analysis.one_liner: Bars states from restricting abortion before fetal viability or when a woman's health requires it.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to protect the right to abortion died in a Senate committee after two days of hearings and never got a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Introduced in late 1989, just months after the Supreme Court's Webster decision gave states more room to restrict abortion, this bill would have made it federal law that no state may ban abortion before the fetus can survive outside the womb, or at any point when an abortion is needed to protect the woman's life or health. States could still impose rules medically necessary to protect the woman's health. It had 26 cosponsors, including 7 Republicans, and was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, which held hearings in March and May 1990 but never voted on it. The bill expired when that Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.who_benefits: Women seeking abortions, especially those in states that would ban or heavily restrict the procedure, and the clinics that serve them, because the bill would override state bans and establish a national floor of access.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women seeking abortions and their providers

how_it_helps.text: No state could restrict abortion before fetal viability, so women in restrictive states would keep access to the procedure.
After viability, abortion would remain legal whenever necessary to protect the woman's life or health.
States could still impose requirements that are medically necessary to protect women's lives or health, so basic health-related regulation would remain possible.

analysis.who_pays: State governments would lose the power to ban or restrict abortion before viability, and the anti-abortion movement would lose its ability to enact those restrictions through state law.

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides state law entirely on pre-viability abortion, removing the ability of state voters and legislatures to set abortion policy through the democratic process.
The health exception is broad, so critics argued it would effectively allow abortion for almost any reason even late in pregnancy, since 'health' can cover psychological well-being.
It would not address access barriers that fall short of bans, such as cost, so the practical benefit for low-income women would depend on other policy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who believe abortion access is a right, the bill offered strong protection with a narrow, medically-grounded carve-out for health regulation, and the main cost was federal preemption of state democratic control. For people who oppose abortion, that cost is the entire point of the bill. Its fatal practical weakness was political: even with bipartisan sponsorship, it never advanced past hearings in a Congress that ended without a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, which held two rounds of hearings but never voted to send it to the full Senate, and it died when the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Senator Alan Cranston introduced the Freedom of Choice Act on November 17, 1989, with 22 original cosponsors including Republicans Bob Packwood, Nancy Kassebaum, John Chafee, Ted Stevens, Pete Wilson, and Bill Cohen.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources the same day.
The committee held hearings on March 27, 1990 and concluded them on May 23, 1990, printing them as S.Hrg. 101-876.
The committee never reported the bill, and the full Senate and House never voted on it before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State governments wanting to restrict abortion and the anti-abortion movement were better off with the bill buried in committee, and members of Congress were spared a floor vote on an abortion bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Abortion-restriction supporters; no one had to vote

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill alongside 19 Senate Democrats, giving it bipartisan support.

against.what_they_did: Held hearings in March and May 1990 but never voted the bill out of committee, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: President George H.W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Opposed the expansion of abortion rights this bill would have enacted, and had no role in advancing it.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so how the chambers would have split is unknown, but sponsorship was bipartisan: 19 of 55 Senate Democrats and 7 of 45 Senate Republicans cosponsored.

industries.note: The bill would have guaranteed a national right to provide abortions before viability and would have voided state bans, protecting clinic operations in restrictive states. Clinics' interest ran alongside patients' interest in access.
The bill would have blocked states from enacting the abortion restrictions these groups push for, including bans before fetal viability.
States, including the District of Columbia and U.S. territories, would lose the power to restrict pre-viability abortion and would be limited to health-related requirements.
